utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. As was announced yesterday to the parties, the Chamber is - and it's very unfortunate, but we can't change it - is unable to sit on Thursday. The Chamber wants to express its appreciation that the Defence was willing to change the order of the next witnesses to be called, which would avoid that two witnesses have to wait for a long time over the weekend because we'll not sit on Friday and Monday either. That's highly appreciated. Then in view of the time indications, that -- we have to stop today at 2.00 sharp. Not any moment later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But in view of the time estimates, the Chamber thinks that it would be possible to finish the witness next to be called in time. I have -- I know that there are a few minor matters which I'll leave for a later moment and let's first continue the cross-examination of the present witness. Good morning, Mr. Lukic, or I should say Professor Lukic, in order to avoid any confusion about whom I'm addressing. Perhaps needless to say but I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And Mr. Traldi will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Are you able to receive interpretation?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday at transcript page 25497 you testified you confirmed that your government conducted a consensus in 1993 and that you personally reviewed the results. Do you recall when you reviewed the results, what month and what year?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. But I know that when they were completed, the results, I had the opportunity to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Were they published?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes. But even if they were not published in the Official Gazette, they were sent out to all the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And they were also shared with members of your government; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And other members of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you confirmed yesterday that you were aware that the census showed that Prijedor had become 96 [Realtime transcript read in error "69"] per cent Serb. The senses showed that the proportion of Serbs in other municipalities in Republika Srpska had also become much higher than it had been in 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember how it was by municipality, but it was probably that because the other peoples left our entity just like our people left the other entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just briefly for the transcript, at page 3, line 1, I am recorded to have said 69 per cent and I believe I said or at least meant to say 96 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Actually, I'd ask that we go into private session, briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 31226. This will be an article from the "Christian Science Monitor" dated the 14th of October 1993. And if we could turn to the second page in both languages, please. And I'm looking at the fourth paragraph in the English and a little bit lower down in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now you're quoted here as saying: "'I personally estimate that when the war is finished, maybe 10 to 15 per cent of the non-Serb population will stay and live in the Serbian Republic ...'" Is that an accurate statement of your position at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what it says, I probably did say it. But I don't remember because, truth be told, I was thinking about how all those who had left Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially those who had left the former Yugoslavia, that it would be difficult for these people to return. Not only because they wouldn't dare but simply because they would be already living in better conditions. I don't know if these two things are connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P6739, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Traldi, you announced 10 minutes yesterday. We are --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, I have one more document to look at, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you testified yesterday that as prime minister, you met with representatives of Serbia and Montenegro. One of the persons you met was the deputy prime minister of Montenegro; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with the two presidents once and I think the deputy, who unfortunately died shortly after.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution have 65 ter 07593. These are the minutes of the 8th Session of the Supreme Defence Council dated the 12th of March 1993. And if we could turn to page 31 in the English and page 26 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the speaker here is Momir Bulatovic, the president of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if we could scroll to the very bottom of the page in B/C/S and just above the number 26 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He says: "The other day, the prime minister of Republika Srpska talked with the deputy prime minister of Montenegro." As of this time, the 12th of March, 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I am. I apologise. I'll read again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He says: "The other day, the prime minister of Republika Srpska talked with the deputy prime minister of Montenegro." As of this time, the 12th of March 1993, you were the prime minister of Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your quotation ended -- oh, now it's corrected in the transcript. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think my next question will, in my view, require a 90(E) information from the Chamber. I'm happy to ask it and wait for the Chamber's view, if that's the Chamber's preference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you -- Witness, would you carefully listen to the next question but not yet answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now turning to page 27, paragraph 1 in the B/C/S. And just below the number 26 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic is speaking and says: "We are obliged to help them. But we are also obliged to understand that we can hardly co-operate with someone who, like the Prime Minister of Republika Srpska, advises us to ethnically cleanse Sandzak and kill the Muslims there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we move to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could just scroll down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, no. I missed that. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What we lost on the page in the English now is Slobodan Milosevic asking "Who says that?" And what we have now at the top of the page is Mr. Bulatovic's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "The Prime Minister of Republika Srpska, Lukic. He advises us to do it as soon as possible, for Muslims are not to be trusted. They will stab us in the back. They will mine our railroad," and so on. My question, and I'd remind you that the Judges had asked you not to answer it yet, my question will simply be whether you recall this conversation as described by Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The reason why I asked you not to answer it yet is because I want to draw your attention to Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and I'll read it to you. It states: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." The question allows for various answers. I do not know the answer. But if a truthful answer might tend to incriminate yourself, and I take it that Mr. Traldi was mainly focusing on the quote where it said that you advised to ethnic cleansing, a truthful answer if that might to incriminate yourself, you may address me and may ask to be relieved from answering that question. The Chamber will then consider how to proceed. I just wanted to inform you that you have that right as a witness. Is it clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's clear, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then would you please -- I'll read again the question that was put to you by Mr. Traldi. The question was whether you recall this conversation as it was described by Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do remember the conversation with Mr. Bulatovic, but the conversation did not proceed in this way. All I said to Mr. Bulatovic was that there were some indications that Muslims from Montenegro were sending -- or actually transferring weapons to Gorazde in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that was our discussion. Because here it seems that he wanted to get in the good graces of Milosevic and that's why he said it, but otherwise everybody knows that I was not a warmonger and I refuse even the idea that I was ever somebody who was supporting ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you recommend or advise Mr. Bulatovic to take any action about the Muslims from Montenegro who you said were transferring weapons?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I said was that it should be controlled because it was threatening us and creating considerable problems. Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So I'd put to you that you did ask Mr. Bulatovic to take action, that you did ask him to control the Muslims in Montenegro that you believed to be a threat. I'd put to you that he has no reason to embellish that story when speaking to the Supreme Defence Council. I'd put to you that his version of the conversation is accurate. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a pure lie. It's immoral. I could not have been speaking about the Muslims of Montenegro. I was talking about the villages that border on Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I said that there were indications that they were sending weapons to Gorazde. This later proved to have been true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise. Your Honours, that completes my cross-examination and I'd ask that this document be, given the length, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P6740 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status for the time being. Mr. Lukic, are you ready to re-examine the witness? I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just need one minute to organise myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll continue for the next session. Branko Lukic, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Lukic, good morning again.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Last time I told you that these were questions that we had for now, but my experience with Mr. Traldi is that he makes us work a lot. He prepares very well, so we need to respond to his questions. So I would like to begin with a document that we can look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at D629 MFI, in e-court please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Professor, these are the minutes of the 66th Government Session held on the 20th of March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 12 in English and page 17 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And questions on this were put to you also by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to look at item 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here you were asked about the Personnel Commission. Could you briefly just tell us what this commission was doing, what was its remit, what were its responsibilities in relation to the municipalities, for example?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I must say that it did not have a great deal of responsibilities, but in any case it reviewed certain questions that were of interest for the government in the area of the economy, administration, education, and so on and so forth. I can say that this commission, during the brief time that it existed, worked very solidly and responsibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the third page in the English and the fourth page in the B/C/S, in this same document. We need to look at item 2 at the bottom of the page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a little bit hard to read it in the B/C/S. I'm going to read it. It says: "The Government noted that the Report of the Ministry of Defence gave a realistic picture of the problems in the financial situation in the Army of Republika Srpska and that the activities and measures indicated for their resolution were good in general." The questions relate to the 66th Session. In the context of the discussion about war booty, when it was suggested to you that the war booty was used for the needs of the army, you said on transcript page 25426, lines 15 on, Judge Orie cautioned you. I'm going to quote now from line 15 onwards: "[In English] Mr. Lukic told me be true. The question of Mr. Traldi is whether this discussion was under the heading of financing problems in the Army of Republika Srpska. So apart from what other financial issues there may have been, but whether this discussion he just referred to, whether that was part of an agenda item about financing problems of the army. "THE WITNESS: Well, the general problems of financing were discussed. Among those topics was also the topic of the army. "JUDGE ORIE: Agenda item 2, I'll read it for you, is reports on the financing problems in the Army of Republika Srpska. Those are specifically focusing on the financing problems of the army." And your answer was: "We were never entirely able to deal with the financing of the army without including everything that I have said previously regardless of whether this was discussed at that meeting or not. This is something that I know very well." And Judge Orie said: "Yes, but Mr. Traldi focuses on this meeting and he'll now continue." [Interpretation] So let's see what the discussion was during this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at page 4 in the English and the 5th page in the B/C/S version of the document. We are interested in item 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which reads: "Urgent reorganisation of the Army of Republika Srpska. The needed number of soldiers must be determined urgently and the surplus reassigned, according to available records, to work obligations in the process of reanimating economic production. In the process, particularly bear in mind exempting professionals who are needed in production from compulsory military service." Was this one of the things you had in mind, Professor, when you said that the issue of the armed forces was always being discussed in a more general context?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That is how we had to approach it, given our situation over all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The document goes on to say: "Define the main task of the army and that of civilian organs, particularly in the domain of the economy. "See to it that everybody, especially the army, state organs and commercial organisations in Republika Srpska is doing their work responsibly and independently." Although this falls under the topic of the army, but does this segment entail the overall picture as well?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Our finances were in such a state that if we discussed the economy it could not go without discussing the armed forces, and if we discussed the armed forces we could not but touch upon other state segments. One always needs to bear in mind that it was in a time of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Item 2 of the same part, referring to the army, which is under item 2 or "ad 2." The document reads: "Take all measures to revive and organise production, particularly in the domain of the special purpose industry. In order to fulfil this task, use personnel who are not crucial for combat operations, and available economic resources, natural resources, etc." While planning economic activities during the war, Professor, did you have to take into account what people were participating in combat and that economic activity was interlinked with military activities?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Although I must say that the economy functioned, to a certain extent, better in the time of war than it does nowadays. The educational system was still intact and operational as well at all levels. Under such circumstances, we paid particular attention to the economy and production. It was our belief that unless the economy was up and running, nothing else would be provided for including the army and civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we go to further detail, let me first see whether there is not some confusion. I think what Mr. Traldi did yesterday was to focus on specific portions of this discussion. And when the witness answered by saying, "Well, this was a kind of general discussion," that Mr. Traldi focused on what the heading of the discussion was. I did not gain the impression that Mr. Traldi was -- that it was his position that financial issues about the army would not be linked to, would not be related to other economic circumstances in society. That was my understanding and apparently, Mr. Lukic, you're now establishing that there were such links and there were interactions between army finance and overall society finance. Therefore, I wonder whether there is any real dispute here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We don't dispute that there were links between the finances of the army and other government institutions, and I hadn't intended to entire about macroeconomic principles or anything of that nature. I'd intended to refer to the agenda item as set out in page 1 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, so therefore please consider to what extent we really have a dispute or not. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will conclude this topic in that case, although I had prepared a number of other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned natural resources yesterday. You mentioned coal, electricity, timber. All of it was interlinked. On some subsequent pages of this document, in particular in item 4, we see the issue of war booty being referenced. Professor, what is war booty? What was considered to be war booty?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you know all too well that in a time of war different things are being seized, plundered, looted, et cetera. However, we only considered war booty to be such items that were not seized by force from any citizen unless it was taken from those citizens who had illegally obtained it and items seized from the enemy. Perhaps this may not include everything in total but in general terms that is what was considered to be war booty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about apartments, houses, and the property of people who resided there, Muslims and Croats, was it also considered war booty?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Private property could not come under the term "war booty" in any case. No one could manipulate it, take it away, or distribute it to anyone including the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next topic, concerning paragraph 56 of your statement. Yesterday, my learned friend, Mr. Traldi, at transcript page 25429, line 16 and onwards, asked you about your assertion that the Muslims in Cerska and Srebrenica painted a fake or a false picture of their situation. You tried to explain something about Cerska when you were interrupted. What kind of information did you have about what the Serb forces in the area came across or found there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that the people in Cerska were starving and that the people who were there could no longer live there. However, our army did enter Cerska. In Cerska, they found cattle, not a single cow but many. They also found other resources. They concluded that the people of Cerska had looted the surrounding Serb villages, at the same time sending out information that they are starving to death. Of course, it was all incorrect. When Mr. Karadzic asked me about it, I conveyed that information to him and he must have used it somewhere. When it comes to Cerska, that is definitely true because it was confirmed to me on several occasions by some officers who had gone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's change tack yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need document P3808 in e-court, please. We're interested in the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Professor, since there seems to have been many exchange commissions in place at the time, there was the central commission for prisoner exchange as well as civilian exchange.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It concerns the 28th of October 1994, as we can see from the document. What kind of prisoner are we talking about here, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not comment upon individual cases that surfaced sporadically, but it is well known that all those kept in prisons were citizens who had committed unlawful acts and were thus imprisoned. Next, I know that there were some cases when civilians were imprisoned. However, I do know of some instances when we reacted immediately and disbanded such locations. Hence, we made a distinction: If the term used was "prisoner," they need not necessarily be criminals but people who committed unlawful acts. The other people involved were simply civilians who were free to go home or to the other side. I just wanted to add something about this commission, although it continued its existence after my departure. Often times, those commissions changed names. You will find it in different places. However, more or less, their task was always the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the answers you're eliciting are all rather general and vague. And as you know, the Chamber has heard about people detained in prison facilities and whether they were civilians or whether they were criminals. Now, these general statements do not add very much to the very concrete information the Chamber has received in evidence presented in earlier stages of this trial. Therefore, I would encourage you where we're looking at documents on specific moments, specific situations, to elicit more than just, "It may have happened this, and then we took action. We do not know, we do not know when, we do not know what action was taken." What we have before us are rather concrete documents. Could you keep that in mind that the Chamber is best assisted by concrete information rather than by statements of a more general nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, you heard what the Chamber is interested in. Right at this moment, can you recall any specific examples when there were attempts made to imprison civilians and when you intervened in order to put a stop to it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several instances when we intervened. I think it was in Rajlovac once, then in Trnovo also once. Next in Banja Luka as well as some other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We demanded to be told the reasons why those people were being imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's take them one by one. Rajlovac. You said there you intervened where there had been civilians imprisoned. How many civilians were imprisoned there and when was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I recall, it was in 1993. I may be wrong, but I recall about a dozen civilians within a greater prison population whose place was not to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they men? Were there women? Were there children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, neither women nor children. Men for the most part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What action did you take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we did was we requested why they were being imprisoned and they were released. The same happened in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did it happen in Banja Luka and about how many --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in Banja Luka it happened in late 1993 or early 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many civilians being imprisoned there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not recall a figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we talking about a few individuals? Are we talking about tens, about hundreds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. When we received such information, it always involved a small number of people or individuals who were in prisons and yet should not have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber received also evidence about larger numbers, and you said, when confronted with those, that it was all exaggerated. I think 10.000 were mentioned for Butmir KP Dom. The -- apparently, the cases you are talking about are about small numbers, whereas the Chamber also received information about larger numbers. Do you have any example of larger numbers of civilians being in prison? And where and what action you took?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't recall such large numbers. As for Butmir, that there were 10.000 civilians there in prison, well, I know the building. There is no way one could fit them all in. Not even close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many could you fit in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly. In any case, I know the size of the building, and it is my estimate that this figure, this many people could not be placed there. There is simply no way. If the number is correct, they must have been out in the open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you mean if they would all have been there at the same time, they would have to be in the open and not housed in the facility itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know whether the civilians held in Butmir prison were kept in the open or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, they were not. That is why I said that there was no room on the premises and that they could only have been in open air. As far as I know, they were not held in the open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's the basis of that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I base it on my presumption that we would have been informed of 10.000 civilians in Butmir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know how long the civilians stayed in Butmir prison? Did they stay there for a week, for three weeks, four weeks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, whether 10.000 were spread over what period of time, you also do not -- you would not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't. As for the figure itself, I don't believe it's true. You can check it. And please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is clear. Yes, Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you said on page 18, you made a distinction if the term used was "prisoner." "They need not necessarily be criminals but people who committed unlawful acts." How am I to understand that? People who were not criminals were in detention and if so, on which basis, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as a rule, and I won't discuss exceptions, but all those who were in prisons, well, there must have been information that they had done something against Republika Srpska or its population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that a legal foundation for imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. I'm not a lawyer. I am only discussing practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You were referring to your own position when you made the distinction between the two groups. You said: "We made a distinction between criminals and those who committed unlawful acts." I would like to know the basis of this distinction you made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps there was a misunderstanding. Criminals were always under the law and they were imprisoned. However, there were also people who were put in gaol when they committed some kind of misdemeanour or infraction and then they were placed in gaol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it your position that, and you had been prime minister at that time, it is lawful to put somebody in a prison where there is no allegation that they have committed crimes but did other things which are not crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't make in a distinction. I did not consider that. In any case, the people involved in it were familiar with the law and acted accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be true for children and women as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under all of our rules, women and children were not imprisoned and could not have been found in gaols.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they accommodated in Butmir prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of that. I don't know of children and women being held in Butmir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Branko Lukic. We'll take a break. The Chamber has taken some time. At the same time, if you allow me to say, Mr. Lukic, again. Mr. Lukic, you may have understood from the questions we are putting to the witness what kind of concrete information this Chamber would like to receive rather than general statements, because going into the concrete makes clearer to us what are presumptions so as if it would have been different we would have been informed. That's a different kind of knowledge as knowledge of personal observation, et cetera. And that's for the Chamber important to know what the evidence is about, what the basis for it is. Would you please keep that in mind. We take a break. The witness may follow the usher. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be brought in, I'd like to deal briefly with the associated exhibits with Witness Vujasin. The Chamber notes that on the 7th of August of this year the Defence indicated it intends to tender 31 associated exhibits to the Rule 92 ter statement of Mihajlo Vujasin. The Chamber notes that two of these documents are already in evidence as P922 and P4281, which then leaves 29 associated exhibits, which is still considerably higher in number than what the Chamber prefers. The Chamber, therefore, invites the Defence to consider reducing the number of associated exhibits by, for example, by tendering some of these documents with the witnesses -- with the witness during his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we prepared for that, so we radically reduced our witness list, and so I believe that we will put forward a maximum of 17 documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still quite a number, but let's move on at this moment. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, we are back again. You are a lawyer and you obviously have different understanding -- you're not a lawyer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- so you obviously have a different understanding of crimes, [In English] and criminals. [Interpretation] Thus, someone who did not report their taxes, would that person be a criminal?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these kind of things were not even considered during the war. A criminal is more completely somebody who stole, who committed killings, who looted, who took things, who raped.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And somebody who caused a car accident and killed somebody, would that be a criminal as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You could consider that a person who had committed a serious offence for which they would be held responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Prekrsaj, it's misdemeanour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Professor, you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- prekrsaj. Let's move on. You said that we were too soft towards women. Women can also commit murder and they would end up in prison for that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. But this is rare. There was a large number of people who did things like that that we couldn't get to, but in any case it was our position that women, children, the elderly, and those who were not armed and who did not commit anything that could make them liable under the law, of course, as a rule, these people were protected. I'm not saying that there were no individuals who violated this principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry for bothering you about these legal matters.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, that doesn't matter. But may I add something? When the war began in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, we had a surge of people coming forward of doubtable moral. They did all kinds of acts, offences, and they were not all from Bosnia and Herzegovina or from Republika Srpska. We had a lot of problems with people like that, of dubious morals, and I'm sure you are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P4008, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Professor, yesterday you were asked about this document dated the 3rd of October 1994. The document was signed by Major-General Zdravko Tolimir. We can see in the first paragraph of the document the agreement that was reached is mentioned. The agreement discuss humanitarian convoys that have made part of the agreement. The same agreement also refers to medical evacuations from Gorazde. The same agreement also talks about helicopter transport of a Muslim delegation from Gorazde to Sarajevo. Evidently, this is a more complex agreement than just a purely exchange agreement. It's evident that Dragan Bulajic was involved in the agreement. He is referred to in the last paragraph of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we could just go to another page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this instance, Dragan Bulajic is exchanging civilians. He's giving civilians; is that correct? Can you see that from this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the document. I've heard of the agreement, but I was not the prime minister at the time. I personally think that it was a good agreement. And as for the mention of civilians, well, they were all civilians more or less, with some possible faults whereby a number of them was detained. But as for such a high number of civilians being detained, well, especially because I am familiar with the situation in Konjac, I know how things came about there. So I did hear of the agreement. I was not prime minister at the time. But I believe that it was a good agreement all in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document D632, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Professor Lukic, this is the presentation of the programme and the make up of the government before the assembly, and this was presented on the 19th of January 1993. My colleague, Mr. Traldi, on transcript page 25445, said that he was going to ask you three things, and then he first referred to pages 1 both in the B/C/S and can the English version. Paragraph 3 states that the statehood is being asked for for the Serbian people. Did the Serbian people already have statehood in the former Yugoslavia and in former Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was Yugoslav statehood. All of us who lived in Yugoslavia had that statehood.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the breakup of Yugoslavia, did others, Muslims, Croats, have to ask for a different statehood than the one they enjoyed in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, because some of them urgently wanted to renounce the Yugoslav statehood. Croats created their own statehood, but they denied that statehood to the Serbs. However in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as you can see, we were left with the BiH statehood, but each of the entities also had their own statehoods. And we know about Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This programme that you presented, did it dispute the statehood of Croats and Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then transcript page 25446, lines 8 to 10, there is a question and an answer when my learned friend Mr. Traldi asked you about other Serbian states. What did you mean, the Krajina and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the Krajina and Serbia, but of course the true state is Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when you were presenting the programme in January 1993, were there already any special links between a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina controlled by Croatian and Muslim forces with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These links existed ever since the beginning of the war, and the war began with those connections in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the first place. I don't need to go into all the different forms of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then on transcript page 25446, lines 11 to 12, my learned colleague Mr. Traldi asked you to look at page 5 of the document in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we will ask to do the same. Page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here the document at the top of the page beginning with, "In the last two years many Serbian families from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Slovenia and Croatia have been left without their homes and hearths. This government must immediately take care of their accommodation and permanent settlement." At the end of the paragraph, it says: [As read] "We have a number of municipalities with very low population density." And then Mr. Traldi asked you on page 25446, lines 20 to 22, and then your answer begins on line 23. It says that the constant displacement of displaced Serbs in the territory of your -- under the responsibility of your government was something that was occurring constantly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will -- I will read from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's all I was going to request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps that's better, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My mistake. I was trying to rush.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Q. Now, permanently resettling displaced Serbs in territory under your government's control was part of your programme as you set it out to the assembly; right?" "A. That is correct." [Interpretation] Let me just ask you this, Professor: Was this project ever implemented? Yesterday you spoke about rich and poor municipalities. Was this ever implemented in practice?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not possible to implement it. It was not implemented in the middle of war to permanently settle those displaced. That is just a nice wish but it wasn't possible. Sir, I just wanted to say three things. I was asked when I was elected prime minister what my programme would be. My programme would be a rule of law, state, the economy, and the front lines. And so my programme, the entire programme, actually, is imbued with these three principles. And this is all that I wanted to say. I just wanted to say that I said this when I was giving my first address once I was elected prime minister-designate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you about something that you just said. The desire to settle border areas of Republika Srpska, was that at the same time a wish to strengthen the front lines?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing to use for strengthening the front lines. We always wanted to strengthen the front lines, that is correct, but it was always done differently. It wasn't done by using refugees who were unprepared both physically and mentally to embark on such a war. This was done in a different way. You heard me say yesterday that I had to tell Mr. Ostojic, "For God's sake, man, we don't have those billions now and we will not have them in peacetime either," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next you were asked about criminal investigations, and it was presented to you that you were biassed and that you were only interested in investigating crimes against Serbs. Through this line of questioning, the Prosecutor wanted to show that you, as the prime minister, as well as the government as a whole, and this is actually the position of our Defence, that you only focused on the welfare of Serbs and that you were not interested in the other two peoples in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please, I have not completed my question. I will show some parts from this same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 6 in the English and 5 in the B/C/S. We're interested in the paragraph beginning with, "Regardless of how vehemently our enemies..." It is the last paragraph in the English and the second paragraph in the B/C/S. In the English version, we'll have to move over to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There you say: "Regardless of how vehemently our enemies insist on continuing this war, we have to insist upon the obligations this assembly has taken over by adopting the declaration on the establishment of peace." Professor, was this just camouflage or did you officially present this to the Serbian assembly as part of your platform?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our position, definitely, and we did not think that continuing the war would bring any good to anyone. As for the refugees, Muslims, and Croats, those who fled went elsewhere. Those who remained had their apartments and houses and they were often in trouble because there were difficulty in them -- their receiving humanitarian aid. Some municipalities simply would not distribute such aid to them and we had to react.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Specifically when did you intervene, since you mention humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Novo Sarajevo. When I arrived in Banja Luka, I know that also some others intervened there. I know that citizens, ordinary citizens also reacted to it. They said that people who were entitled to a pension should receive it irrespective of ethnicity, and those entitled to receiving humanitarian aid should be treated the same. That was a more general position of all and that is what we stood for.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. We have a document on the list of documents we have tendered which would corroborate that. As for the VRS, when you presented your programme, was it in favour of peace?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It absolutely was. I know that for several reasons. I'm particularly familiar with the army position when tens upon tens of thousands of central Bosnia Croats were supposed to traverse Mount Vlasic to reach the lower part of the Bosna River and on to Banja Luka. Those Croats from Vares, Olovo, and Kakanj were also allowed to go through Sokolac and Pale and the entire eastern part of our territory to move to their territory in Stolac. Without our armed forces would not -- it would not have worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was some agreements concluded between the Croat and Serb side at the time concerning the cessation of hostilities. What was the position of the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we drafted a very fair agreement with the Croats. We freed all prisoners, all-for-all, irrespective of who was held in those prisons, and we gave signals for the Muslim side to join us. Mr. Prlic and I were frankly in favour of that as well as some other people. However, they did not want to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next topic you discuss, and it ties in with the previous sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version it begins with, "This means ..." This is the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me read it out. "This means that we must persistently and patiently look for solutions to our common exploitation of water, electric power, roads, and so forth, the care for patients in medical institutions, the regulation of the status and exchange of prisoners, the use of documentation indispensable to pensioners and other citizens when claiming entitlements stemming from work relations and so forth." Professor Lukic, who did you have in mind when you say "common"? Did you have only in mind the Serbs or all ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All ethnicities. One cannot divide water, forests, and other such things. A civilised society cannot be organised on any side unless the use of such resources is approached jointly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will continue reading from this paragraph. In presenting your programme, that is to say the future of the RS government to the RS Assembly, and as far as I understand, it was only populated by Serbs at the time, the assembly that is, you say the following: "Already today we must begin creating conditions so that citizens who have left their homes because of war, because they did not feel safe and felt their property was threatened, once permanent peace has been established, can return to the territory of Republika Srpska. We must guarantee to all citizens of other ethnicities all rights under the Constitution and laws. We have taken these obligations upon us and we have to fulfil them." Professor, on that occasion, did you only have the Serbs in mind or all of the ethnicities residing in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It never even occurred to me to refer to the Serbs alone. I referred to the nationals of Bosnia and Herzegovina or rather the nationals of Republika Srpska who were there at the time as well as the return of those who left, in order for them to return safely and be able to exercise their rights just like any other citizen. Counsel, let me add this: Republika Srpska did the most in that regard when it comes to the return of refugees. Just look at the figures of how many refugees returned to the federation. You will soon realise, if you did so, that we were the best in implementing this goal in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we end up, Mr. Branko Lukic, in speeches again without any details on matters not asked about, which would serve well, perhaps, in a political debate, could you please more strictly guide the witness in answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll probably deal with specifics and numbers with our democratic expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm not against. But we did better look at the numbers. If we don't have the numbers and if we do not know what to look at exactly is -- is not of great assistance to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, have you received support by members of the government for your programme? For this programme that you presented to the RS Assembly, did you receive the support of government members?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was a draft programme. As you well know, a draft is created first when putting together a programme. Once it was all ready, we consulted and presented it to President Karadzic and those most senior in the armed forces as well as some other experts for whom we believed could be of assistance. In other words, the programme as a whole received support from the assembly as well as in the course of drafting from a wide circle of people who had the occasion to read it and later support it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any army representatives at the assembly?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any assembly session was attended by army representatives, especially when this programme was being adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anyone ask you to change the government programme in this part that we have read out here?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The programme was adopted as a whole. There were no votes against it whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will switch topics now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have D638 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of April 1993, you were rather critical vis-à-vis the army. As we can see here, you informed the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska - that is to say, the body headed by General Mladic - as well as the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps that the government of Republika Srpska was informed of looting, killing, setting fire to buildings, and rape in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo committed mostly by members of the Army of Republika Srpska. Yesterday you explained that you reacted whenever there were any signs of this or any information.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've already explained that yesterday. Thank you. I wanted to ask you the following: Regarding this and similar documents, did anyone ever order you or asked you to -- or kindly asked you to hide things if you ever learned of a crime or any irregularity?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: God forbid. You know me and you know that I'm not a person who would easily be manipulated, especially when it comes to crime, rape, looting, et cetera. Among other things, you saw that I discussed looting with Mr. Mladic. Not so that we would boast but so that we would each do something within our remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the reaction to this and similar caution by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long time ago and I can't recall every detail, but I can say that any suggestion or proposal on our part to this effect was something they objected to. They always said that they would see to it that they would do something. I could frequently observe that the army acted responsibly in that regard in introducing order in society, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P6733 MFI on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were shown this letter yesterday. It's in English. That is why it was only marked for identification. In the letter signed by Mario Mobilo, some allegations are spelled out against the Serbian side. Who did Mario Mobilo represent on the 9th of January 1993, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I know that very often he would act irresponsibly, like a prosecutor, even though he was not a side in the conflict regarding the Serbian side and was aware of crimes on his own side. He did not mention any of those and spoke without any restraint about the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi asked you yesterday if you had heard of accusations that there were 60.000 Muslim women who had been raped. Now I'm going to ask you this: Did you hear later and do you know that it was established that this was pure wartime propaganda?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the record and the clarity of the witness's answer, I don't think I referred to a number. I referred to the text referring to mass rapes on the second page of this document and -- so I don't think my question's been presented accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, did you hear of charges that there were 50- or 60.000 Muslim women who were raped by Serbs in the first few months of the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But I heard also Silajdzic's statement that there were 250.000. A foreign journalist heard with a man from our area that there were 5.000 raped women at the stadium in Tuzla. They set off there and then halfway there he was told not 5.000 but 1.000. And then when they came close to Tuzla, he was told, well, it wasn't really that many. And then finally when they got there, it turned out that there were some 10 or 15 women who had been raped and not the thousands that were mentioned before. So this is just pure insinuation. Actually, it's propaganda that was supposed to prompt people to feel sorry for Muslims and to condemn the evil Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And are you aware that during the first few month of the war, it was said that some 250.000 to 300.000 Muslims had been killed?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did wonder where they managed to find so many Muslims in that area when there weren't even that many there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear later that this turned out to be propaganda as well?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. And it was not just that, there were many other things that were part of the wartime propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You talked about the return of refugees and that you only meant the refugees -- the return of Serb refugees. This was something you discussed with Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that we cannot prove.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Is it correct that towards the end of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbs were being arrested in Serbia and being brought to Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could have been individual cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't hear of any mass arrests in that sense. I don't know about that. I know that a number of recruits were rounded up. I don't know if this occurred on a major extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic -- perhaps I first ask the witness: When you said "I didn't hear of any mass arrests in that sense," were you talking about mass arrests of Serbs or were you talking about mass arrests of Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no Croats or Muslims there enough for any kind of mass arrests. This was -- this had to do with the Serbs from Republika Srpska. This is who I was talking about, Serbs from Republika Srpska who were being arrested there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to be that you are so focused on what apparently seems important to you that -- no, let me just see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question was in relation to Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's closure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And maybe I wasn't clear. Maybe I wasn't clear enough. But what I wanted to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Mr. Traldi was on his feet. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I was. I wasn't sure how the arrests of persons in Serbia, particularly conscripts, arose out of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My intention was to show voluntarily return of anybody to Vares or to war zone in Bosnia. Because the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, when talking about arrests that are not voluntarily returning but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly. There was none on any sided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was none on any side. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But that should be my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, was there a mass return of Serbs to Republika Srpska during the wartime years, refugee Serbs from Croatia, from Bosnia and Herzegovina? How many them would return to the combat zone in Bosnia and Herzegovina before the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever they were able to avoid the combat zone, they would avoid it. So only when they didn't have anywhere else to go would they remain in the combat zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So neither Serbs nor Muslims nor Croats would return to the combat zone?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not then. As a rule they did not return. Perhaps some individuals did but otherwise no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we just look at three documents briefly that were shown to you today by my colleague, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need 65 ter 31188. I don't see that it was tendered, so the document doesn't have a P number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a document under seal, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ah, that's why maybe. Okay. Then shouldn't be broadcasted. Should we go to a private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what questions you want to put about it. But perhaps out of an abundance of question we should --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, it should be dealt with only in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're waiting for the document. There are both versions in English and B/C/S. That's good. We need page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here you can see in the seventh paragraph with the words, "Personally ..." And the paragraph says the following: "'I personally estimate that when the war is finished maybe 10 to 15 per cent of the non-Serb population will stay and live in the Serbian Republic,' admits Vladimir Lukic." And then it goes on to say: "The self-styled Bosnian Serb prime minister." Is this correct? That you were the self-styled prime minister of Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't have appointed myself the prime minister of Republika Srpska. This was done upon the proposal of President Karadzic. I was elected by the assembly. So I'm not even going to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And would you consider this text as objective or partial -- or impartial?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the same thing as that thing that Mr. Bulatovic says. I don't think I would like to comment too much on this. All I would like to say is that really this is no way to go about it. It's not a good thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for the rest of the sentence, I don't know whether that refers to you or not, because it says: "Witnesses say between 40 and 50 Muslims are expelled every few days by Bijeljina's state commission for the exchange of civilian population headed by Vojkan Djurkovic a Major in the Serbian Tigers, the most notorious of the old Serb paramilitary bands."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that, but if that came to us, we definitely immediately reacted. That was the first thing. This was abolished. That could not have continued to operate. And let me tell you this: We had many self-styled people who were involved in exchanges and many other things so that it was not easy to catch all of them and to deal with all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Professor, I promised that I would leave some time towards the end to my colleague Mr. Traldi, so that would be all that I have for you at this time. Thank you very much. I don't know if I have left enough time for my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you -- I think you stayed well within your estimates, Mr. Lukic, which is appreciated. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd need just a little bit less than ten minutes probably, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that we will continue and take the break after that. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: First, the document that we have on the screen. Could we go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'm just going to ask you to confirm that you can see the date 14 October 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that should be the date. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P2047. This is a code cable sent by Mr. Akashi. I'm going to be interested in the third page in both languages, which is an attachment to the code cable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So just now you said you would have immediately reacted if you'd known what Mr. Djurkovic was doing. Now here we read a letter from Nicholas Morris of the United Nations HCR to President Karadzic, and it's dated the 5th of September, 1994. It reads: "Already this month, over 1300 members of the minority communities in the Bijeljina and Janja area have been forced to leave their homes by your authorities and expelled towards Tuzla. Similar departures continue from the Banja Luka region to Croatia: almost 1.000 in the last two weeks. The expulsions from the Bijeljina area are combined with the exaction of significant sums of money (reportedly by a man known as 'Vojkan')." And I'll stop there. I'd put to you first that that Vojkan is the Vojkan Djurkovic referred to in the article from the previous year that we just saw. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that is the same person. I don't know that there is another Vojkan. But I personally don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So I put to you what this shows is that no one reacted immediately. And in fact, a year after the interview that Mr. Lukic showed you or the article that Mr. Lukic showed you, Mr. Djurkovic was still expelling people from Bijeljina. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You have shown me a letter to Karadzic of the 5th of September. I was not prime minister at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: All right. Then I'll turn to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can 65 ter 16580 be brought to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to add something to your question. At the time, I was in Banja Luka. When the Serbs were expelled from 12 Krajina municipalities, one of the soldiers with his wife and another friend -- actually, while I was at university, he wanted to expel my wife from her apartment. So at that time, many Serbs in Banja Luka, not just the Muslims and Croats, were exposed to threats, and I was a witness of that. At one point in time, I had the impression that there were more refugees in Banja Luka than the citizens of Banja Luka. Precisely because --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- there was these 12 municipalities --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- you've gone far beyond the scope of my question. This document refers to minority communities. In Bijeljina and Banja Luka, Serbs were the majority; right? Simply yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then I'm going to turn to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 16580. And this will be a document from the JNA 5th Corps on the 11th of May 1992 entitled: "An Order to Take-over War Booty."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At temporary transcript pages 16 and 17 today, General Mladic's counsel asked you about war booty, and you testified that "private property could not come under the term war booty in any case." Now in this document, directing your attention first to point 1, it refers to making a list of all motor vehicles from war booty. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then at point 2 it says: "Take the rest of the war booty (women's jackets, plastic canisters, refrigerator parts, etc.) From the 30th Partisan Division to Major Zdjelar in the Kozara barracks for safe keeping." So these items are being treated as war booty by the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably so. But I am not familiar with these details. I only know what we talked about, war booty in general. Now, whether someone took a jacket and where they put them is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P6741, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, can P6722 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: While it comes up, you were asked by the Chamber and the Defence whether civilians were detained in Bosnian Serb prisons. Do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, here we have a prisoner exchange report from the Bosnia-Herzegovina State Committee for Exchanging Prisoners of War.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have page 4 in the English and 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We're looking at a list of persons that the Serb side did not release in an exchange. I just want to direct your attention to number 11, Hanka Kustura. And it says: "According to the Serbian side, she died at the age of 101 while in the Rogatica-Rasadnik prison." So my question to you is simply were you aware that civilians, including elderly women were being detained in Rasadnik prison?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that and I'm not even aware of the existence of a prison in Rogatica, in Rasadnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Finally, could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 02395. This is the transcript of the 41st Session of the RS Assembly. And I'll ask for the bottom of page 50 in the English and 46 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, Minister Brdjanin, one of the two ministers in charge of the refugee programme, is speaking. And I want to direct your attention to the third sentence in his remarks. He says: "First of all, gentlemen, you cannot fool me that you believe in the greatest wonder of the world such as that Brdjanin could participate in a process of return of Croats and Muslims." Now, none of your refugee ministers ever said no one could believe they would take part in a process of return of Serbs to the Republika Srpska, did they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot discuss this because I don't remember it. If it's in the document, it is probably true. I think, though, that you were able to observe in your trials here who Brdjanin is and who is Ostojic and what things they said. I guarantee you, and any responsible official in Republika Srpska would confirm it, that not a single proposal of theirs was implemented anywhere. Given the fact that Ostojic is no longer among the living, I didn't want to discuss him. And Brdjanin is where he is. He did have a fault, though, because once he was at the lectern, he simply could no longer control himself. That's the kind of person he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question for you. You've, on almost all the questions which were relevant for either the Defence or the Prosecution, you immediately jumped to things that were done to the Serbs. You very much emphasized that you are better than anyone else in returning other -- in returning refugees to Republika Srpska. You said a lot of good things about your performance. Do you at all admit that serious crimes, sometimes massive crimes, were committed by Serb units, police forces, army forces, killing sometimes a large number of people? Do you say this is also exaggerated? It is also -- it's not true, it's propaganda. And let me just, because I asked the parties to be concrete, let me take one concrete example. This Chamber heard evidence about events at Koricanske Stijene. Do you say that's propaganda or is it, in your view, true that these type of crimes were committed, and I'm not saying that similar crimes are not committed by others, but those type of crimes, massive crimes, were committed by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Koricanske Stijene, I heard about it upon my arrival in Banja Luka. Bear in mind that I had lived in Sarajevo for 37 years. During the war, I did not go around Bosnia-Herzegovina. I could only draw conclusions on the basis of the things I heard. As for the existence of crimes on our side as well, I never denied that. It is interesting, though, that only Serbian crimes are being studied and referred to, leaving aside the other parties. I don't even want to start discussing the number of crimes which took place in Sarajevo. I know of crimes against Muslims being committed in Sarajevo, but of even greater number of crimes against Serbs. Unfortunately, there is no war without crime, especially not in our region where hatred originates from a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You again emphasize that -- how important it is apparently for you is to strike a balance between who did what, and you claim that no attention was paid to crimes committed by others than Serbs. Now I leave that alone. You have not directly answered my question. Koricanske Stijene, close to 200 victims, executed, as we heard evidence of, I'm not saying that it happened, but we heard evidence of that and in other cases the matter was dealt with extensively. Do you agree that that happened or I asked you whether you considered this propaganda or exaggeration or whether you accept that - and I take that as an example - happened?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You chose the right example. I said that it was only in September 1994 that I heard about Koricanske Stijene. Unfortunately, it is true. I inquired about it and I received precise responses from the people who heard or saw it. Hence, there is nothing for me to add or subtract. And I don't want to take anything away, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for answering my question. Yes, Mr. Lukic, you have one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just two questions. And first we need P6741.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
